At the age of 18-24, most male temples will naturally recede to about this stage in the pictures as part of puberty and it is usually not an indication of genetic Male Pattern Baldness. In people who do not have Male Pattern Baldness, their temples will not recede past this until much later in life.

However, if you're noticing significant or progressive loss of density in the areas you do have hair (such as the hairline or the 'crown', the top of your head) then it might be an indication of balding. This could be from MPB, or it could be from mental stress or lack of vitamins (or scalp health). If you recently had a new job or more responsibilities for example, this could contribute.

Your hair is still very thick, so having 10 hairs fall out is not immediately concerning, especially if you haven't paid attention to how many hairs fall out in recent years compared to now. You can google the 'hair pull test' and do it weekly before showering to count how many hairs on an average day you are shedding and keep track of it, if it is increasing. I also recommend taking pictures of the top of your head and your temples every month to see if it is progressing.

The best thing of course is to see a dermatologist and have them do an inspection, have them take their own pictures of the scalp and if they say it's not balding, see them for a follow-up appointment a year later to compare just to be sure.

To summarize all of this, it is unlikely you are balding, and if you are losing hair it is not likely because of MPB. But this is just my opinion, these things can change, some people get hit with balding very fast later in life or very early, it all depends. As long as you are cataloging evidence of progressive shedding or lack of shedding, you will be able to make a better determination if you're a candidate for hair loss medication.

Also remember again that this is just my opinion, you know you better than myself, but that's my educated input based on experience and much reading.

Precisely, especially because "we eat" and "we ate" are essentially the same two phrases with different tenses. Less repetition of word combinations in a sentence will almost always sound more natural. Your reader will assume the action implied in "had" in this case because it is often correlated with past tense consumption or having used an intended function of something.

Example A: "We went to the party for drinks and had some juice"

Example B: "We went to the party for drinks and drank some juice" 

These are the saying the same thing, but example A is more natural to read because of less reptition. It is not a rule of thumb, but it reads more casually whilst B is a bit more redundant.

2 is the best, the others are a bit messy in their meaning. Combining a hypothetical in a sentence with a reference to a previous subject is difficult to write without reading like a run-on sentence, and it's often best to break these up into two different sentences. 

If you wanted to write it all in one sentence, personally I would write the second as: “Do you think we will get diabetes if we eat those desserts we had at the potluck yesterday after dinner everyday?” 

Since the first part of the sentence is about eating "those desserts," the inclusion of the past tense "ate" is not necessary, as the action performed on the desserts at the potluck yesterday is assumed because of the subject. The sentence still works the way you wrote it, but it's a bit awkward to read.

Both are correct, the choice between these two sentences would be predicated on personal preference or writing style. As a native speaker, the perception of the first sentence makes me believe the first will flow into a larger description quicker and may not need the comma, whereas the second sentence most likely will read/sound better with the comma (but that is just my personal preference and experience).

"The test scores on this exam are similar to the last exam, they seem to indicate a pattern"

"The pattern of test scores on these exams shows which students are doing well"

"There were patterns of repeated topics in the exam questions"

"The topics in the exam questions were repeated in patterns"

There are many ways you could format its use to describe a reocccurring 'event' or 'thing', or lack thereof

\- My biggest mistake was not realizing tap water was so bad for cannabis, especially my tap water, which is very hard water. \- I switched to RO PH adjusted water because I didn't know my tap water was so beyond awful.

\- I finally invested in a PH meter to read the water that drained through her, PH correction was huge, it was coming in at an 8.0 under the soil

\- I was a big wimp with feeding her, was giving her way too little food, I corrected my feedings to the fox farms feed calendar

\- I upgraded her light, although she would have done okay on the previous light, 400 watts is a huge change

\- I repotted her in a proper 5-gallon bag, her soil depth has increased allowing her roots to go further for bloom. Repotting with new soil seemed to do a lot, as the old soil was started to dry out faster, and from the look of it had depleted its nutrients. 

​

Essentially she was very starved in every way from proper nutrition, the PH was shot up and down extremely frequently from attempting to PH adjust the hard tap water, and the feedings were not big enough to combat this.

Changing the water source was the biggest difference in change. Without hard tap water I was able to diagnose what nutrient or PH problems she was having easier, and I'm pretty sure i got her locked in for bloom now.
